name: Grade 12
theme: Vocation, faith in the world and the last things

units.title: Discerning your vocation
units.eq: What does God ask of me?

lessons.title: Every person is called
lessons.idea: God calls every person to holiness and to a particular way of life. Vocation begins with Baptism and unfolds through discernment: prayer, the sacraments, the Church’s guidance and honest self-knowledge. Jeremiah’s call shows that God knows and chooses us before we do.
lessons.question: How do I discern?
lessons.activity: “Vocation journal” (40 min). Students start a four-part journal: gifts (what I do well), joys (what gives me life), needs (what the world needs that I notice) and invitations (moments I sensed a call). They write a first entry on each and name one trusted person to discuss it with.
teach: All are called to holiness (CCC 825, 2013; Lumen Gentium 40). Each also has a particular vocation within the one mission of the Church (CCC 1877–1879, 897–933).
God’s call is personal: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). It comes through gifts, circumstances, desires purified by prayer and the Church’s discernment.
Discernment uses Ignatian tools: notice consolations and desolations, pray with Scripture, seek spiritual direction, test in action (CCC 2690).
Reassure students: God does not hide his will; a vocation is a gift to be received, not a puzzle to solve alone.
quiz: Which statement best separates the universal call from a particular vocation?|Only priests and religious have a vocation|Everyone is called to holiness; a vocation is the particular way a person lives it|A vocation is a career choice made once at 18|The universal call applies only to the baptized who are confirmed|1|CCC 825, 2013 and CCC 1877–1879: holiness is for all; each lives it in a state of life.

In Ignatian discernment, “desolation” is best described as…|Any sadness, which proves a choice is wrong|The end of prayer|A sign that God is angry|A movement toward discouragement and away from faith, hope and love|3|It is a movement away from God; it must be read with care and counsel, not by mood alone.

Jeremiah 1:5 (“before I formed you…I knew you”) is used in this lesson to show that…|God’s call precedes our choosing and invites a free response|God’s plan is a secret code to be cracked|Doubt disqualifies a person|Vocations are fixed by birth order|0|God takes the initiative; we respond freely (CCC 2232).
lessons.saint: Ignatius: a soldier turned priest whose Spiritual Exercises teach discernment.
misc: “A vocation means the priesthood or religious life.”
“If I choose wrong, I have ruined God’s plan.”
lessons.mem: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you.” (Jeremiah 1:5)
lessons.hook: Read Jeremiah 1:4–8 aloud. Ask: “What excuse does Jeremiah give? What does God answer?” Students name excuses they use when something feels too big.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the difference between the universal call to holiness and a particular vocation, and name one step in discernment.

lessons.title: Marriage, priesthood, consecrated life, single life
lessons.idea: The Church recognizes four ways of living out the call to holiness: marriage, the ordained priesthood and diaconate, consecrated life, and single life lived for God. Each is a real vocation with its own graces and challenges, and each needs the others.
lessons.question: What are the criteria for discernment?
lessons.activity: “Interview someone in each vocation” (45 min). Over a week, students interview a married person, a priest or deacon, a consecrated religious and a committed single person. They ask: How did you know? What is the hardest part? What surprised you? Present findings in a one-page comparison.
teach: Marriage is a covenant and a path of holiness for the couple and children (CCC 1601–1666). Holy Orders configures a man to Christ the head and servant (CCC 1536–1600).

Consecrated life lives the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience as a sign of the Kingdom (CCC 914–933). Single life can be a gift of availability when chosen for God, and also a circumstance that is lived in faith.
None is “higher” in dignity; each is higher in what God asks of that person (CCC 1620). Vatican II teaches a universal call to holiness.
Pray for vocations. Discernment is communal as well as personal.
quiz: Which statement best reflects Church teaching on marriage and consecrated virginity?|Both are optional for Christians|Marriage is a lesser, merely natural state|Marriage is a sacrament and a real path to holiness, and the Church also esteems virginity for the Kingdom as a special sign of the life to come (CCC 1619–1620)|Only celibates are called to holiness|2|CCC 1619–1620 and CCC 2013: each state of life is a way of holiness; neither is outside the call.
The evangelical counsels are…|Poverty, chastity and obedience|Fasting, prayer and almsgiving|Prudence, justice and fortitude|Faith, hope and charity|0|CCC 915.

A single person who lives for others and prays faithfully is…|Excused from holiness|In a waiting room until marriage|Not part of the Church’s mission|Living a real vocation if it is a gift offered to God and neighbor|3|The call to holiness belongs to all; single life can be a vocation.
lessons.life: Talk with someone in a vocation.
lessons.saint: Francis: who gave up wealth to follow Christ in poverty and joy and loved creation.
misc: “Marriage is the default; priesthood and religious life are rare exceptions.”
lessons.mem: “Each has his own special gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.” (1 Corinthians 7:7)
lessons.hook: Read 1 Corinthians 7:7: “Each has his own gift from God.” Ask: “Why would Paul say that both marriage and celibacy are gifts?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe each of the four states of life and what each witnesses to.

lessons.title: Work and gifts
lessons.idea: Work is part of God’s plan: humans share in his creative work and sanctify the world by it. A vocation includes how we use our gifts for others. Work has dignity, and workers have rights.
lessons.question: How can work be holy?
lessons.activity: “Reflect on a career” (40 min). Students write about a career or field they are considering, answering: How could this serve others? What would it ask of me morally? What could go wrong? Where could I be a Christian witness? Pair up and share.
teach: Work is a duty and a way to participate in God’s creative work (CCC 2427). Laborem Exercens (John Paul II): work is “for man,” not man for work.
Rights of workers: just wage, safe conditions, rest, the right to organize (CCC 2433–2436). Employers have duties of justice (CCC 2434).
Rest is part of God’s plan: Sabbath (CCC 2184–2188). Work must not become an idol.
Vocation includes how we love in daily work: “Whatever your task, work heartily, as serving the Lord” (Colossians 3:23). St Joseph the Worker is a model.
quiz: In Catholic teaching, the primary reason work has dignity is that…|It earns money|The worker is a person made in God’s image, and work shares in God’s creative action|It keeps people busy|The state requires it|1|CCC 2426–2428; Laborem Exercens.
Which of these is a right of workers named in the Catechism?|A guaranteed promotion|A ban on all employers|A just wage and the freedom to organize|Exemption from all risk|2|CCC 2434–2435.

Why does the Church insist on rest (Sabbath) alongside work?|Because people are more than their productivity, and rest orders life toward God and others|Because work is evil|Because rest earns salvation|Because laws forbid factories|0|CCC 2184–2188.
lessons.saint: Josemaría Escrivá: a priest who taught that ordinary work, done for love, can make us holy.
misc: “My job is just a way to make money.”
lessons.mem: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.” (Colossians 3:23)
lessons.hook: Read Genesis 2:15 (“to till it and keep it”). Ask: “Was work a punishment or a gift?” Work existed before the fall; toil was added by sin.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain a Christian view of work and apply it to a career path.

units.title: Faith and culture
units.eq: How does faith meet the modern world?

lessons.title: Faith and science
lessons.idea: Faith and reason are two wings by which the human spirit rises to the truth (Fides et Ratio). Because God is the author of both, genuine science and faith cannot conflict. When they seem to, we have misread one of them.
lessons.question: Is evolution compatible with faith?
lessons.activity: “Study Fides et Ratio” (45 min). Students read excerpts from John Paul II’s encyclical (1998) and summarize: the dangers of fideism and rationalism, the role of philosophy, and the call to seek truth. Then take a case (Galileo, evolution, the Big Bang and Fr. Lemaître) and show how faith and science interact.
teach: “Even though faith is above reason, there can never be any real discrepancy between faith and reason” (CCC 159). The same God who reveals mysteries has endowed the human spirit with reason.
Methodical research in every branch of knowledge, when carried out in a truly scientific manner, “never conflicts with faith” (CCC 159; Gaudium et Spes 36).
Fr. Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, proposed the Big Bang theory. Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, founded genetics. Many scientists have been believers.
Scientism, the claim that only empirical science yields truth, is itself a philosophical position, not a scientific result.
talk: How do you respond to claims of conflict?
What is the role of philosophy?
quiz: A believer says, “If I just follow the science, I must give up faith.” What does the Church’s teaching in Fides et Ratio say?|Reason is the enemy of faith|Faith and reason are two wings; truth cannot contradict truth|Science and faith have separate truths that conflict|Only faith matters|1|CCC 159; Fides et Ratio opens with the two-wings image.

Scientism is the claim that…|Faith can answer scientific questions|Science is a good gift|Only what can be measured empirically is real or knowable|Scientists should be religious|2|It is itself a philosophical claim that science cannot prove.

Which person shows that a Catholic priest has contributed to modern science?|Descartes, a bishop|Darwin, a monk|Galileo, who was a priest|Georges Lemaître, who proposed the big bang|3|Lemaître was a Belgian priest and physicist; Mendel, an Augustinian friar, founded genetics.
lessons.saint: Albert the Great: a Dominican scientist and bishop, patron of scientists, who taught Aquinas.
lessons.mem: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims his handiwork.” (Psalm 19:1)
lessons.hook: Show the opening line of Fides et Ratio: “Faith and reason are like two wings.” Ask: “What happens to a bird with one wing?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how faith and reason relate and respond to an alleged conflict.

lessons.title: Atheism and secularism
lessons.idea: The Church engages unbelief with honesty and charity. Atheism takes many forms: practical atheism, agnosticism, scientism, and secularism. The Church listens, asks why, and offers the reasons for hope. Believers also bear some responsibility for unbelief.
lessons.question: How do we respond to atheism?
lessons.activity: “Debate” (45 min). Teams argue the question “Can one be good without God?” One side takes a Christian view of grounding morality in God; the other presents a secular case and its strengths. Afterwards they list where they found common ground and where the real disagreement lies.
teach: Atheism is one of the gravest problems of our time (CCC 2123–2126; Gaudium et Spes 19–21). It has diverse forms: denial of God, agnosticism, indifference, scientism, ideologies.
Believers can contribute to unbelief when they present a distorted image of God (CCC 2125). A credible witness and genuine dialogue are needed.
Secularism separates public life from faith; the Church distinguishes healthy secularity (autonomy of earthly affairs) from secularism (excluding God).
Engage with respect. Listen to what people have suffered or doubted. Offer reasons: the contingency of the world, the moral law, beauty, Christ.
quiz: The Catechism says believers can contribute to atheism when they…|Present a distorted picture of God or fail to live the faith credibly (CCC 2125)|Pray too much|Study philosophy|Attend Mass|0|CCC 2125.
Practical atheism means…|Worshiping nature|Denying God by argument|Being agnostic by principle|Living as if God does not matter, even without denying him|3|CCC 2125.

Paul’s approach in the Areopagus (Acts 17) models…|Silence about Christ|Avoiding philosophy|Starting from what listeners already believe and then proclaiming the Gospel|Condemning the crowd first|2|He cites their altar and their poets before announcing the resurrection.
lessons.life: Listen to a skeptic with charity.
lessons.saint: Edith Stein: a philosopher who came to faith through reason and died at Auschwitz as a Carmelite.
lessons.mem: “Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence.” (1 Peter 3:15)
lessons.hook: Read Acts 17:22–31. Ask: “How does Paul begin his speech to the Athenians? What does he start from?” He starts from their own search.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe three forms of unbelief and how to engage each charitably.

lessons.title: Pluralism and religious freedom
lessons.idea: The Church affirms religious freedom as a right rooted in human dignity: no one may be forced to act against conscience or prevented from acting in accord with it, within just limits. Faith must be free, and the Church defends this freedom for all people.
lessons.question: What is religious freedom?
lessons.activity: “Study Dignitatis Humanae” (45 min). Students read key paragraphs (DH 2–4) and summarize the argument. They then map current cases of religious persecution and restriction around the world and discuss what believers and governments should do.
teach: Vatican II’s Dignitatis Humanae (1965): the right to religious freedom is based on the dignity of the human person (CCC 2104–2109). Faith is a free act and cannot be coerced.
This right is for everyone, including non-Christians. The state must protect it, within just public order. The Church also claims freedom to carry out her mission.
The teaching develops earlier practice: the Church acknowledges that coercion in matters of faith was sometimes wrongly used in history.
Religious freedom is increasingly threatened: Christians are among the most persecuted groups worldwide.
talk: Why does the Church defend it?
quiz: According to Dignitatis Humanae, religious freedom is grounded in…|Indifference about truth|The state’s permission|The dignity of the human person, who must not be coerced in matters of conscience|The majority’s will|2|CCC 2106; DH 2.

Which statement is true?|The Church has never changed its practice on coercion|The Church teaches that all religions are equally true|The Church teaches that no one may be forced to act against conscience in religion, within just public order|Religious freedom means faith is private only|2|The teaching is firm and its application has developed.

“My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36) is cited because it shows…|Christ’s mission is not advanced by force|Faith must be hidden|Christians should avoid politics|The state has no authority|0|The Gospel is proposed, not imposed.
lessons.saint: John Paul II: the pope who taught on love and the body, and who prayed with leaders of many faiths.
misc: “Religious freedom means all religions are equally true.”
lessons.mem: “My kingdom is not of this world.” (John 18:36)
lessons.hook: Read John 18:36 (“My kingdom is not of this world”). Ask: “Why did Jesus refuse to fight?” The Gospel is proposed, not imposed.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the foundation of religious freedom and one global application.

units.title: Catholic social teaching in depth
units.eq: How do we build a just society?

lessons.title: Subsidiarity and participation
lessons.idea: Subsidiarity holds that decisions should be made at the lowest level able to handle them, with higher bodies helping but not replacing. Participation means every person has the right and duty to contribute to the common good. These two principles protect freedom and community.
lessons.question: What is subsidiarity?
lessons.activity: “Case study” (40 min). Provide a scenario (a school district, a parish, a city) where a central authority has taken over local decisions, or where local groups are neglecting a need. Students apply subsidiarity: who should decide? Who should help? Where is intervention justified?
teach: Subsidiarity: “a community of a higher order should not interfere in the internal life of a community of a lower order, depriving the latter of its functions” (CCC 1883; Pius XI, Quadragesimo Anno).
It also requires higher bodies to help when lower ones cannot cope (CCC 1884–1885). It guards against both individualism and collectivism.
Participation: all citizens have a right and duty to take part in public life (CCC 1913–1917). Voting, serving, volunteering, informed engagement.
Show examples: the family before the state, the parish before the diocese, local charity before national programs.
talk: How does it apply to school?
quiz: The principle of subsidiarity says…|Decisions should be made at the lowest level able to act well, with higher bodies helping when needed|All decisions belong to the largest body|Local groups may ignore the law|The state should do everything|0|CCC 1883–1885.

Which situation violates subsidiarity?|A national agency takes over a function a local community could perform well|A city helps a school in need|A diocese coordinates parishes|A parish asks a family to help|0|The higher body replaces what lower bodies can do.
Participation in public life is…|A right and a duty according to one’s role (CCC 1913–1917)|Optional for Christians|Reserved to officials|Forbidden to clergy only|0|CCC 1913–1917.
lessons.saint: Dorothy Day: a journalist who founded the Catholic Worker movement to serve the poor.
lessons.mem: “Just as the body is one and has many members… so it is with Christ.” (1 Corinthians 12:12)
lessons.hook: Read 1 Corinthians 12:14–20. Ask: “What if the head did everything and the hands did nothing?” Introduce subsidiarity.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define subsidiarity and apply it to a concrete case.

lessons.title: Economic life
lessons.idea: Economic life exists to serve the person. The Church teaches the dignity of work, a just wage, the right to private property with a social purpose, the rights of workers to organize, and care for the poor. Rerum Novarum began a long tradition of social teaching on economics.
lessons.question: What is a just wage?
lessons.activity: “Reading Rerum Novarum summary” (45 min). Students read a summary of Leo XIII’s 1891 encyclical. They identify: what it rejects (socialism’s abolition of property, unregulated capitalism), what it affirms (private property, a just wage, unions). Then apply to a modern case: gig work, minimum wage, remote work.
teach: Work is for the person; the economy must serve people (CCC 2426–2428). Economic life is subject to moral law (CCC 2423–2425).
Just wages enable a family to live with dignity (CCC 2434). Workers have the right to strike in just circumstances and to form unions (CCC 2435).
Private property is legitimate but has a “universal destination of goods” (CCC 2402–2406). Charity does not replace justice.
Later documents (Quadragesimo Anno, Centesimus Annus, Caritas in Veritate) address globalization, markets and the common good.
talk: What is the universal destination of goods?
What is the role of business?
quiz: Catholic social teaching about private property holds that…|It belongs only to the state|It is evil|It is legitimate yet bound by the universal destination of goods|It is absolute|2|CCC 2402–2406.

Rerum Novarum (1891) is notable because it…|Rejected all labor unions|Defended workers’ rights, a just wage and private property against both socialism and unrestrained markets|Was addressed only to priests|Endorsed communism|1|Leo XIII.

A just wage is, in the Church’s view, one that…|The market sets, whatever it is|Allows a worker to support a family with dignity (CCC 2434)|Equals what the employer likes|Is the same for everyone in all jobs|1|CCC 2434.
lessons.life: Read the opening of Rerum Novarum.
lessons.saint: Frédéric Ozanam: a student who founded the St Vincent de Paul Society to serve the poor of Paris.
lessons.mem: “Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out; and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.” (James 5:4)
lessons.hook: Read James 5:1–6 on wages held back. Ask: “What does James condemn? What does it say about how God sees workers?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state four principles of Catholic economic teaching.

lessons.title: War and peace
lessons.idea: The Church promotes peace as “the tranquility of order” and holds that war is always a failure of humanity. She also teaches that use of force may be legitimate in strictly limited conditions of defense, when just war criteria are met. Peacemakers are blessed.
lessons.question: What is just war?
lessons.activity: “Study” (45 min). Students study the just war criteria (CCC 2309): lasting, grave damage by an aggressor; all other means impractical; serious prospects of success; no greater evils produced. They then evaluate a historical case against the criteria and discuss the role of conscientious objectors.
teach: Peace is “the tranquility of order” (Augustine; CCC 2304) and requires justice and charity. “Blessed are the peacemakers” (CCC 2305).

All citizens and governments are obliged to avoid war; yet governments have the right of legitimate defense (CCC 2308–2309). The conditions for just war are strict; the means must also be just (CCC 2312–2314).
Conscientious objection is respected (CCC 2311). Arms race, terrorism, torture and indiscriminate destruction are gravely wrong (CCC 2314–2317).
Recent popes have asked whether war can still be justified given modern weapons. The Church supports nonviolent peacemaking.
quiz: Which is among the conditions for a just war (CCC 2309)?|Lasting, grave and certain damage inflicted by an aggressor, with all other means shown impractical|The enemy is of another religion|The ruler wishes it|It would be profitable|0|CCC 2309.

The Church’s teaching on conscientious objection is that…|It is always wrong|The law should provide for those who refuse to bear arms, if they serve in another way (CCC 2311)|It applies only to priests|It is required of all|1|CCC 2311.
Peace, in the Catechism’s phrase, is…|The mere absence of war|The tranquility of order (CCC 2304)|Impossible on earth|A feeling|1|Augustine’s definition; peace requires justice and charity.
lessons.saint: Francis: who gave up wealth to follow Christ in poverty and joy and loved creation.
misc: “Just war means any war our side declares just.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” (Matthew 5:9)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 5:9: “Blessed are the peacemakers.” Ask: “Is peace the same as the absence of war?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to list the just war criteria and apply them to a case.

lessons.title: The sanctity of life
lessons.idea: Every human life is sacred from conception to natural death because each person is made in God’s image. Direct abortion and the intentional killing of the innocent are gravely wrong, and the Church calls for help for mothers, families and everyone in need.
lessons.question: Why from conception?
lessons.activity: “Research” (45 min). Students research the science of fetal development, local pregnancy-help services and Church teaching (Evangelium Vitae). They produce a one-page brief that presents the Church’s argument, how to respond to common objections, and ways to support women in crisis. Respect those with painful experiences.
teach: Human life is sacred from conception until natural death (CCC 2258, 2270–2271). Abortion is a grave moral evil (CCC 2271); formal cooperation incurs excommunication (CCC 2272).
Science: a unique human organism with its own DNA begins at fertilization. The Church’s argument is based on human dignity, not only on faith.
The Church also teaches compassion: Project Rachel offers healing for post-abortion pain; pregnancy centers and parishes can support women (CCC 2274–2275).
Respect for life also includes the poor, migrants, the disabled and the elderly (Evangelium Vitae 87).
talk: How do we respond with compassion?
quiz: The Church’s case against abortion rests mainly on…|The dignity of every human person from conception, which reason can recognize, and the commandment against killing the innocent|A single verse|Politics alone|Medical preference|0|CCC 2270–2271.

Which response best reflects the Church’s pastoral approach after an abortion?|Mercy and healing available through Confession and ministries such as Project Rachel (CCC 2279)|Despair|Silence|Blame|0|The Church offers forgiveness and accompaniment.

Which is part of defending life “from conception to natural death”?|Ignoring the dying|Only opposing abortion|Also caring for the poor, the sick, migrants and the elderly|Leaving it to the state|2|Evangelium Vitae links all.
lessons.saint: Gianna Molla: a doctor and mother who chose her baby’s life over her own.
misc: “The Church only cares about unborn life.”
lessons.mem: “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb.” (Psalm 139:13)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 139:13–16. Ask: “What does this say about when a person begins to matter to God?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to present the Church’s case and how to support women in crisis.

lessons.title: End of life
lessons.idea: Euthanasia and assisted suicide are morally unacceptable because they directly end a life. The Church also allows refusing burdensome treatment and strongly supports palliative care. Suffering has meaning in Christ, and the dying deserve accompaniment.
lessons.question: What is dignified death?
lessons.activity: “Case studies” (45 min). Present three cases: a terminally ill patient requesting assisted suicide, a family deciding on withdrawing ventilators, a hospice patient receiving palliative sedation. Students analyze using the distinction between ordinary and extraordinary means and between intending death and accepting it.
teach: Euthanasia — an action or omission that of itself or by intention causes death in order to eliminate suffering — is morally unacceptable (CCC 2277). Assisted suicide is also gravely wrong (CCC 2282).
Discontinuing disproportionate or burdensome treatment is legitimate (CCC 2278). Pain relief, even if it shortens life, is acceptable if death is not intended (CCC 2279).
Palliative care is a preferred form of charity. Hospice care honors the dying.
Suffering is not good, but united to Christ’s Passion it can be redemptive (CCC 1521, 1505). Accompany the dying with love, presence and the sacraments.
talk: What is ordinary vs extraordinary care?
How do we accompany the dying?
quiz: Which is morally acceptable according to the Catechism?|Direct euthanasia to relieve pain|Refusing disproportionate or burdensome treatment (CCC 2278)|Assisted suicide|Intentionally ending life with an overdose|1|CCC 2277–2279.

Palliative care that relieves pain even if it may shorten life is acceptable when…|The aim is to cause death|The patient is old|Death is not willed or intended and the means are proportionate|It is secret|2|CCC 2279.

Why does the Church say suffering can have meaning?|Because it is unavoidable|Because pain is good|Because united with Christ’s Passion it can be redemptive, while we still work to relieve it|Because God sends it to punish|2|CCC 1521.
lessons.saint: Camillus: a former soldier who founded an order to care for the sick.
misc: “The Church requires keeping people alive at all costs.”
lessons.mem: “Jesus wept.” (John 11:35)
lessons.hook: Read John 11, the raising of Lazarus. Ask: “What does Jesus do at the tomb? What does he feel?” He weeps. The Church does not minimize suffering.
lessons.assess: Ask students to distinguish euthanasia from refusal of burdensome treatment with examples.

lessons.title: Bioethics and technology
lessons.idea: The Church engages new technologies in medicine, biology and computing. She asks of each: Does it respect the dignity of the person? Is the person treated as a subject or as an object? The Church supports science that heals and opposes what degrades human life.
lessons.question: How do we judge technology?
lessons.activity: “Debate” (45 min). Teams debate a motion: “Gene editing of human embryos should be banned.” Use principles: dignity, the common good, the difference between therapy and enhancement. Consider related topics: artificial intelligence, organ donation, stem cells. Write a guiding question to ask of any new technology.
teach: Scientific research is a noble service when it respects human dignity (CCC 2292–2296). Experiments on human beings must respect their rights and consent.
Organ donation is praiseworthy when free and not harmful (CCC 2296). Embryonic stem cell research is wrong since it destroys embryos; adult stem cell research is licit.
Reproductive technologies that separate procreation from the marital act are wrong (CCC 2376–2377). Gene therapy for healing is allowed; eugenics and enhancement raise grave questions.
Artificial intelligence and data raise questions of privacy, work and the human person (Rome Call for AI Ethics; Antiqua et Nova).
talk: How do we judge new technologies?
What is the role of conscience?
quiz: A Catholic test for a new technology starts with the question…|Is it profitable?|Is it new?|Is it legal?|Does it respect the dignity of the person as a subject rather than a thing?|3|CCC 2292–2296.

Which is a licit use of stem cells according to Church teaching?|Cells taken from adult tissue or umbilical cord blood without harming a human embryo|Cells taken by destroying embryos|Any use if it cures|None|0|The Church supports ethical stem-cell research.

Why does the Church warn about “designer babies”?|It dislikes medicine|It is unsafe only|It treats a child as a product to be chosen and risks eugenic discrimination|It forbids all genetics|2|CCC 2377–2379.
lessons.saint: Gianna Molla: a doctor and mother who chose her baby’s life over her own.
misc: “The Church is against all new technology.”
“If we can do it, we should.”
lessons.mem: “Give me wisdom, that sits by your throne.” (Wisdom 9:4)
lessons.hook: Read Wisdom 9:1–6, the prayer for wisdom. Ask: “What does Solomon ask for? Why is wisdom needed with power?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to propose three questions to ask of any new technology.

units.title: Other Churches and religions
units.eq: How does the Church relate to others?

lessons.title: Eastern Churches and the Orthodox
lessons.idea: The Orthodox Churches and the Eastern Catholic Churches are very close to the Catholic Church: they share apostolic succession, valid sacraments, the Creed and devotion to Mary and the saints. The main differences concern papal primacy and jurisdiction, the Filioque and some doctrines.
lessons.question: What are the differences?
lessons.activity: “Visit an Eastern church” (60 min). Attend a Divine Liturgy (or watch a recording). Students note: the iconostasis, incense, chant, the priest’s role, the epiclesis, communion with leavened bread. Afterwards they list what felt familiar and what was new, and write a note of thanks.
teach: The Eastern Churches possess true sacraments, especially the priesthood and Eucharist (CCC 838, 1399–1400; Unitatis Redintegratio 14–18). Catholics may receive Communion in Orthodox churches in some circumstances when no Catholic ministers are available, as the Code of Canon Law provides.
Differences: authority of the Pope, the Filioque, purgatory, the Immaculate Conception, divorce and remarriage.
Eastern Catholic Churches are in full communion with the Pope, with their own rites, canon law and married priests.
Pope John Paul II’s “two lungs” image and Ut Unum Sint call for continued dialogue.
talk: What do we share with the Orthodox?
quiz: The main differences between the Catholic and Orthodox Churches concern…|Papal primacy and jurisdiction, the Filioque and some later doctrines|The existence of the sacraments|Baptism|The Creed’s first line|0|CCC 838; Unitatis Redintegratio 14–18.
An Eastern Catholic Church is…|A schismatic body|A Protestant group|A Church in full communion with Rome that keeps its own rite and discipline|An Orthodox Church|2|CCC 1203, 1399.

Why does the Catholic Church call the Orthodox Churches “sister Churches”?|They use Latin|They accept the Pope|They have true sacraments and apostolic succession|They share the same calendar|2|CCC 838, 1399.
lessons.saint: Josaphat: a Ruthenian archbishop and martyr who worked for unity between East and West.
misc: “Orthodox and Catholics are totally different religions.”
“Reunion would require one side to surrender.”
lessons.mem: “That they may all be one.” (John 17:21)
lessons.hook: Read John 17. Ask: “What does Jesus pray for? How might the Churches heed that?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state three points of agreement and two of difference between Catholic and Orthodox.

lessons.title: Protestant communities
lessons.idea: Protestant communities share with Catholics Baptism, Scripture and faith in Christ, but differ on authority, the sacraments, ministry and justification. The Church speaks with respect and works for unity.
lessons.question: What do we share?
lessons.activity: “Study Unitatis Redintegratio” (45 min). Students read UR 19–24 and summarize what it says about Protestant communities: elements of truth, genuine Christian life, differences, and the invitation to dialogue. Compare the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999) with Reformation-era disputes.
teach: Those who are baptized and believe in Christ are in a certain, though imperfect, communion with the Catholic Church (CCC 818–819). Their communities possess elements of sanctification and truth.
Differences: sola scriptura vs. Scripture and Tradition; papal authority; the Eucharist; Mary and the saints; seven sacraments vs. two or three.
Ecumenism includes prayer, theological dialogue, shared service. The Church recognizes Protestant Baptism if properly done with water and the Trinitarian formula (CCC 1256).
Avoid proselytizing; witness with charity and clarity.
quiz: What shared ground does the Church recognize with Protestant communities?|None|The papacy|The Mass|Baptism, Scripture and faith in Christ (CCC 818–819)|3|CCC 818–819.

The 1999 Joint Declaration on Justification showed that Catholics and Lutherans…|Share a basic consensus on justification by grace through faith while some differences remain|Denied grace|Were in schism still|Agree on everything|0|Joint Declaration.
Which is a real Catholic–Protestant difference?|Belief in Jesus|Baptism with water|The authority of Scripture alone versus Scripture with Tradition and the Magisterium|Belief in God|2|CCC 80–82.
lessons.saint: John Paul II: the pope who taught on love and the body, and who prayed with leaders of many faiths.
lessons.mem: “There is one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism.” (Ephesians 4:4–5)
lessons.hook: Read Ephesians 4:1–6. Ask: “What does Paul call us to?” Unity in one body.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain common ground with Protestants and two real differences.

lessons.title: Judaism, Islam and other religions
lessons.idea: The Church honors the Jewish people as the people of the first covenant, esteems Muslims who worship the one God, and respects what is true and holy in other religions. She calls Catholics to dialogue and to reject all anti-Semitism and hatred.
lessons.question: How do we dialogue?
lessons.activity: “Interreligious conversation” (60 min). Invite guests or visit a synagogue, mosque, or other house of worship. Prepare respectful questions. Afterward reflect: what did we share? What distinguishes our faith? How can we cooperate for good?
teach: The Church recognizes the Jewish people as God’s first-called people. “To them belong the sonship, the glory, the covenants” (Romans 9:4). Anti-Semitism is a sin against the Gospel (CCC 839–840; Nostra Aetate 4).
Muslims profess the faith of Abraham and worship the one merciful God. We share much, though we differ about Christ and the Trinity (CCC 841).
Other religions contain rays of truth (CCC 843–845). The Church’s mission remains to proclaim Christ, with respect for freedom.
Catholic–Jewish and Catholic–Muslim dialogues continue.
talk: What do we share with Jews?
quiz: Nostra Aetate teaches that the Jewish people…|Must be avoided|Remain beloved of God, whose gifts and call are irrevocable (Romans 11:29)|Are collectively guilty|Have been replaced by the Church|1|CCC 839–840.

Which sentence best captures the Church’s view of other religions?|They are to be ignored|All are equal|They contain nothing true|The Church rejects nothing true and holy in them, and still proclaims Christ|3|CCC 843; NA 2.
Interreligious dialogue, for the Church, is…|A part of mission that listens and bears witness with respect|Only for experts|Forbidden|A replacement for mission|0|CCC 856.
lessons.saint: Charles de Foucauld: a hermit who lived among the Tuareg of the Sahara in simple friendship and prayer.
lessons.mem: “For the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.” (Romans 11:29)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 11:1–2, 11:29. Ask: “What does Paul say about God’s gifts to Israel?” “Irrevocable.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Church’s attitude toward Jews, Muslims and other religions.

units.title: Apologetics: giving a reason
units.eq: Why do Catholics believe what they believe?

lessons.title: Scripture and authority
lessons.idea: Sola scriptura (“Scripture alone”) is the claim that the Bible is the sole authority. Catholics respond with Scripture and history: Scripture itself points to Tradition and the Church, the canon was set by the Church, and a pillar of truth is needed to settle disputes.
lessons.question: How do we respond?
lessons.activity: “Use the Apologetics section” (45 min). Students use the Apologetics section of the app. For each of three objections (“sola scriptura is biblical”, “traditions of men”, “Catholic traditions contradict the Bible”), they gather verses (2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Timothy 3:15; 2 Peter 1:20; Matthew 15:3–9) and historical facts (the canon) and write a concise reply.
teach: Scripture and Tradition together form the deposit of faith (CCC 80–82). 2 Thessalonians 2:15 commends oral and written traditions. 1 Timothy 3:15 calls the Church “the pillar and bulwark of the truth.”
2 Timothy 3:16–17 says Scripture is “profitable,” not that it is “sufficient alone.” The canon itself was determined by the Church’s Tradition.
Jesus condemned human traditions that contradict God’s commands (Mark 7:8), not apostolic tradition.
Be fair: Protestants hold to the high authority of Scripture and many regard creeds and confessions as authoritative. Dialogue calmly.
talk: How do you respond to sola scriptura?
quiz: Which is the strongest reply to “the Bible alone is our authority”?|Tradition replaces Scripture|The canon itself was recognized by the Church, and the New Testament points to oral tradition and to the Church as the pillar of truth|Scripture is unimportant|The Bible is false|1|2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Timothy 3:15.

2 Timothy 3:16–17 says Scripture is “profitable.” A careful reply notes that it…|Says Scripture alone suffices|Denies Scripture|Does not claim Scripture alone is sufficient, only useful|Applies only to the New Testament|2|Profitable does not mean sufficient alone.
The Catholic view of Tradition is that it…|Is only written|Is the living transmission of the Gospel, not a second source that contradicts Scripture|Is optional custom|Adds new revelation|1|CCC 80–82.
lessons.saint: Francis de Sales: bishop and doctor who taught that holiness is for everyone in every state of life.
lessons.mem: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.” (2 Thessalonians 2:15)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Where does the Bible say ‘the Bible alone’?” Open 2 Timothy 3:16 and read carefully. Ask what it says and does not say.
lessons.assess: Ask students to give a concise reply to sola scriptura with two Scriptural and one historical point.

lessons.title: The Eucharist and the saints
lessons.idea: The Real Presence and the intercession of the saints are two doctrines often challenged. The biblical and patristic evidence for them is strong: John 6, the words of institution, 1 Corinthians 10–11, and the early Church’s practice of honoring martyrs.
lessons.question: What is your best argument?
lessons.activity: “Practice” (45 min). Pairs role-play a friendly conversation: one raises an objection (“Isn’t communion just a symbol?”; “Why pray to saints?”), the other responds with Scripture (John 6:53–56; 1 Corinthians 11:27–29; Revelation 5:8) and Fathers (Ignatius, Justin, Cyril of Jerusalem). Switch roles and give feedback on tone.
teach: The Church believes in the Real Presence on the basis of Christ’s words and the unanimous witness of the early Church (CCC 1374–1376). Ignatius (c. 107): “the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ.”
The saints intercede for us (CCC 956–957; Revelation 5:8, 6:9–10). The early Church honored martyrs’ tombs and asked for their prayers (catacomb inscriptions).
Avoid proof-texting. Show the whole pattern of Scripture and Tradition.
Always remember the person: a good answer is gentle and patient.
talk: How do you respond to objections?
quiz: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107) matters for the Real Presence because he…|Wrote after the Reformation|Called the Eucharist “the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ”|Denied it|Never mentioned it|1|Letter to the Smyrnaeans 7.

A Protestant friend says asking saints to pray is idolatry. A good Catholic answer begins by…|Avoiding Scripture|Quoting only Mary|Distinguishing worship due to God alone from asking fellow members of Christ’s body to pray for us (CCC 956–957, 2683)|Dismissing the objection|2|Veneration is not adoration.
Which verse supports the saints’ intercession by showing heavenly beings offering prayers?|Psalm 23|Genesis 1:1|Revelation 5:8|Romans 3:23|2|Revelation 5:8; 6:9–10.
lessons.saint: Justin Martyr: a philosopher who became a Christian and described the Mass around the year 155.
misc: “Early Christians saw the Eucharist as a symbol.”
lessons.mem: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.” (John 6:53)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If you were to prove to a skeptic that Christians have always believed in the Real Presence, what would you show?” List the sources.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present a two-minute answer to an objection about the Eucharist or saints.

lessons.title: Confession and the papacy
lessons.idea: Two common objections concern Confession (“Why go to a priest?”) and the papacy (“Why is Peter the rock?”). John 20:21–23 and Matthew 16:13–19 are central, and the early Church’s practice supports the Catholic understanding.
lessons.question: How do we respond with charity?
lessons.activity: “Role-play” (45 min). In trios (questioner, responder, observer), students practice answering: “Only God can forgive sins” and “Peter is just a pebble (petros) not the rock (petra).” Use Mark 2:7–10, John 20:23, the Aramaic “Kepha,” Isaiah 22:22, and early testimonies (Clement, Ignatius, Irenaeus, Cyprian). Observers give feedback.
teach: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive sins in his name (John 20:21–23; CCC 1441–1442). “God has reconciled us to himself and given us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).
The papacy: Peter is the rock (Matthew 16:18), receives the keys (Isaiah 22:22; Matthew 16:19), confirms his brothers (Luke 22:32) and feeds the flock (John 21:15–17) (CCC 881–882).
In Aramaic Jesus said “Kepha” for both Peter and the rock. Early Fathers acknowledge Rome’s special authority (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3).
Present the doctrine of papal infallibility accurately (see earlier grades).
talk: How do we answer with charity?
quiz: In John 20:21–23, Jesus…|Tells the apostles to avoid sin|Gives the apostles the power to forgive and retain sins|Appoints a single scribe|Forbids confession|1|CCC 1441–1442.

The Aramaic “Kepha” in Matthew 16:18 helps answer the claim that Peter is just a “pebble” because…|It is not mentioned|It means pebble|Jesus likely used the same word for Peter and the rock|It is Greek|2|The Greek petros and petra reflect the Aramaic kepha.

Which best describes papal infallibility?|The Pope is sinless|The Pope, teaching definitively on faith or morals to the whole Church, is preserved from error (CCC 891)|Whatever he says is infallible|It applies to politics|1|CCC 891.
lessons.life: Practice explaining the papacy in 2 minutes.
lessons.saint: Peter: a fisherman who denied Jesus and was forgiven, and became the first pope.
misc: “The priest forgives by his own authority.”
lessons.mem: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them.” (John 20:22–23)
lessons.hook: Read John 20:21–23 and Matthew 16:18–19. Ask: “What power does Jesus give? To whom?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to answer one objection about Confession and one about the papacy.

lessons.title: Death and judgment
lessons.idea: Death ends our earthly pilgrimage. Each person is judged by Christ immediately after death (particular judgment) and again at the end of time (general judgment). Hebrews 9:27: “It is appointed for men to die once, and after that comes judgment.” This is a call to live now with love.
lessons.question: How should we prepare?
lessons.activity: “Reflect” (40 min). Students write a reflective piece on the Church’s teaching on death and judgment, ending with a short examination of conscience and a list of what matters most. Offer silent prayer and, if desired, the Prayer for a Happy Death.
teach: Death is the end of earthly life and the entrance to eternal life (CCC 1005–1014). Christ transformed death: for believers, it is a participation in his death and resurrection (CCC 1006–1009).
The particular judgment: “Each man receives his eternal retribution in his immortal soul at the very moment of his death” (CCC 1022). The general judgment will reveal all (CCC 1038–1041).
We are judged on love (Matthew 25). Mercy and justice meet in Christ (CCC 679).
Remember to speak gently with students who have lost loved ones. Memento mori is spiritual practice, not morbid fear.
quiz: Hebrews 9:27 (“appointed for men to die once, and after that comes judgment”) is used to rule out…|The resurrection|Prayer|Reincarnation|Heaven|2|CCC 1013.
The particular judgment happens…|Only for saints|Never|At the end of time|Immediately after death, when each soul receives its eternal destiny (CCC 1022)|3|CCC 1022.
What will the general judgment reveal?|Only the sins of the wicked|Nothing new|Only Church history|The full meaning of history and of God’s justice and mercy (CCC 1040)|3|CCC 1038–1041.
lessons.life: Write a letter to your future self about eternity.
lessons.saint: Joseph: patron of a happy death.
lessons.mem: “It is appointed for men to die once, and after that comes judgment.” (Hebrews 9:27)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If you had one year to live, what would change?” Take answers. Then read Hebrews 9:27.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the particular and general judgment and how they shape life now.

lessons.title: Heaven, hell and purgatory
lessons.idea: After death, those who die in God’s grace and friendship and are perfectly purified live forever with him (heaven). Those who die in God’s friendship but need purification undergo purgatory. Those who freely and finally refuse him choose hell. The Church knows these as realities, not as maps.
lessons.question: What is purgatory?
lessons.activity: “Study” (45 min). Students read CCC 1023–1037 and compose a three-column summary: heaven (vision of God, communion), purgatory (purification, prayer for the dead, 2 Maccabees 12:45), hell (self-exclusion, the reality of freedom). Add a pastoral reflection on how the Church prays for the dead.
teach: Heaven is “the ultimate end and fulfillment of the deepest human longings” (CCC 1024). The blessed see God face to face (CCC 1023–1029).
Purgatory is a final purification (CCC 1030–1032). The Church prays for the dead and offers Masses, alms and indulgences for them.
Hell is a state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God (CCC 1033–1037). God predestines no one to hell. The Church canonizes saints but never declares anyone damned.
Rather than speculation, the Church stresses hope and conversion.
quiz: Purgatory, according to the Church, is…|A second chance after death for those who rejected God|A place of eternal punishment|A final purification for those who die in God’s friendship but still need holiness (CCC 1030–1031)|A myth|2|CCC 1030–1032.

Hell is described in the Catechism as…|A place that must be earthly|The state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God (CCC 1033)|A natural disaster|God’s decision to punish|1|CCC 1033, 1037.

Why do Catholics pray for the dead?|To change God’s mind|Because the Church on earth can help those being purified (2 Maccabees 12:45; CCC 1032)|Because it is required for salvation|To be superstitious|1|CCC 1032.
lessons.saint: Catherine of Genoa: a laywoman and hospital worker who wrote about purgatory as love’s purification.
misc: “Purgatory is a second chance after death.”
lessons.mem: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him.” (1 Corinthians 2:9)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 16:19–31, the rich man and Lazarus. Ask: “What does the story warn about? What does it show about ongoing relationship?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain heaven, purgatory and hell and their pastoral implications.

lessons.title: The new creation
lessons.idea: Scripture ends with the promise of new heavens and a new earth where God dwells with his people. Creation will be transformed and the body will rise. Christian hope is not escape from the world but its renewal.
lessons.question: What is the hope?
lessons.activity: “Meditation” (40 min). Students pray Revelation 21 slowly, imagining the scene. They list images and connect each to Genesis (tree of life, river). They write a short prayer of hope and reflect on how this vision affects work for justice and care for creation now.
teach: At the end the universe will be renewed: “a new heaven and a new earth” (CCC 1042–1050; Revelation 21:1). Our bodies will rise glorified (CCC 988–1004).
The vision of God, communion of saints and life with the Trinity are the fulfilment of human desire (CCC 1023–1029).
Christian hope motivates work in the world: “earthly progress must be carefully distinguished from the growth of Christ’s kingdom” yet it can contribute (CCC 1049).
The liturgy anticipates it: the Mass joins heaven and earth.
quiz: Christian hope for the “new heavens and new earth” implies that…|Creation will be renewed and transformed (CCC 1042–1050)|Matter is evil|Time will repeat|Creation will be destroyed|0|CCC 1042–1050.

The resurrection of the body means…|The body is lost forever|The soul alone survives|The whole person, glorified, will be raised, as Christ was (CCC 988–1004)|People return as new animals|2|CCC 988–1004.

Which attitude toward work and justice follows from this hope?|Fear|Effort to build up the world now, since earthly progress can serve the Kingdom without being identical with it (CCC 1049)|Indifference|Withdrawal from the world|1|CCC 1049.
lessons.saint: John: the beloved disciple, who stood at the cross and wrote a Gospel and Revelation.
misc: “The material world will be destroyed and forgotten.”
lessons.mem: “Behold, I am making all things new.” (Revelation 21:5)
lessons.hook: Read Revelation 21:1–5. Ask: “What is new? What is missing?” The story ends with a city and a garden.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe the new creation and how it influences present action.

units.title: Mission
units.eq: How do I live my faith now?

lessons.title: Lay mission
lessons.idea: Laypeople are the Church in the world. Through Baptism they share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly mission, and their special vocation is to sanctify the world from within: in family, work, culture and public life.
lessons.question: What is my mission?
lessons.activity: “Write a mission statement” (45 min). Students write a one-page personal mission statement for their lay vocation: values, relationships, work, parish, service. They name three concrete commitments and a person who will hold them accountable.
teach: The laity “seek the kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and directing them according to God’s will” (CCC 898; Lumen Gentium 31). Apostolicam Actuositatem (the Decree on the Lay Apostolate) elaborates this.
They share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly office (CCC 901–913). They can also serve in parish ministries.
Examples: St Thomas More (politics), St Gianna Beretta Molla (medicine, motherhood), Blessed Frédéric Ozanam (charity), St Josemaría Escrivá (sanctifying work).
Avoid clericalizing the laity. Their mission belongs to them by Baptism.
talk: What is the mission of the laity?
quiz: Lay people share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly mission by…|Only joining parish committees|Taking over clerical duties|Staying out of society|Consecrating the world from within through work, family and civic life (CCC 898–900)|3|CCC 898–913.
Which is an accurate description of the laity’s role?|Active members with a mission of their own by Baptism|Servants of clergy only|Passive|Optional in the Church|0|CCC 897–913.

An example of lay holiness in public life is…|An angel|Jerome, only a hermit|Francis, who rejected all work|Thomas More, who served as a statesman and died for conscience|3|Examples of lay sanctity in public life.
lessons.saint: Pier Giorgio Frassati: a young Italian who served the poor and went to Mass and adoration daily, and died at 24.
misc: “The laity’s role is to pray, pay and obey.”
lessons.mem: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 5:13–16 (salt and light). Ask: “Where are you called to be salt and light this year?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to present their mission statement and one commitment.

lessons.title: Prayer for life
lessons.idea: A rule of life is a realistic plan for daily and weekly practices that keep a person close to God: Mass, Confession, daily prayer, Scripture, service, rest, and community. It brings structure so love can grow.
lessons.question: What is my rule?
lessons.activity: “Create a rule of life” (45 min). Students draft a rule with daily (Morning Offering, Scripture, Angelus or short prayer, Examen), weekly (Sunday Mass, a service act, a rest day), monthly (Confession, a retreat or spiritual reading), yearly (a retreat). They share it with a friend or mentor and set a review date.
teach: A rule of life gives order and consistency to the Christian life, as in religious orders and in lay associations (CCC 2030). It should be realistic, flexible and revisable.
Prayer is essential: “pray constantly” (1 Thessalonians 5:17; CCC 2742–2745). The sacraments, especially Eucharist and Penance, nourish. Scripture forms mind and heart.
Acts of service and rest keep the rule balanced. Spiritual direction helps keep it honest.
Teach perseverance: relapse and restart are normal. Grace comes before and after effort.
talk: What do you need in a rule?
quiz: A good rule of life is best described as…|A rigid set of rules to earn salvation|An optional hobby|A realistic, flexible plan of practices that supports love of God and neighbor|A secret code|2|CCC 2030, 2044.
Which element is essential in any Catholic rule of life?|Silence|Weekly Sunday Mass and regular sacramental life|Daily fasting|Travel|1|CCC 2042–2043.
What should you do when you fail to keep your rule?|Blame others|Give up|Hide it|Begin again without drama and adjust it|3|The goal is love, not perfection.
lessons.saint: Benedict: the father of Western monasticism, whose Rule says, “Prefer nothing to the work of God.”
misc: “Anything less than an hour of prayer a day doesn’t count.”
lessons.mem: “Pray without ceasing.” (1 Thessalonians 5:17)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 18:1: “Jesus told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart.” Ask: “What helps you keep a habit?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to present their rule and explain how it supports love of God and neighbor.

lessons.title: Sending forth
lessons.idea: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.” As graduates and young adults, students are sent. The Church’s mission is carried out by missionary disciples who witness with their lives and words, wherever they go.
lessons.question: How will I go?
lessons.activity: “Commissioning” (45 min). Hold a simple commissioning rite: reading, a moment where each student names their commitment aloud, a blessing, the Sending Forth, a prayer. Provide a symbolic gift (a cross, a small Bible, a prayer card). Close with a hymn.
teach: The Church is missionary by nature (CCC 849–851; Ad Gentes 2). Evangelization includes witness of life, proclamation, dialogue, works of charity (CCC 2044).
Pope Francis (Evangelii Gaudium) speaks of “missionary disciples.” Every Christian is both disciple and missionary.
Go with humility, joy, courage and openness. The Spirit goes before.
Remain connected to the Church community: parish, campus ministry, young adult groups.
quiz: What does Pope Francis mean by “missionary disciples”?|Clergy only|Every baptized person is both a follower and a sent messenger|Only professional missionaries|Persons who travel abroad|1|Evangelii Gaudium 120.
The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20) includes…|Go, make disciples, baptize, teach, and the promise “I am with you always”|A command to avoid people|Only teaching|Only baptizing|0|Matthew 28:19–20.
Which approach to sharing faith fits Catholic teaching?|Imposing|Witness, gentleness, truth and respect for freedom (1 Peter 3:15; CCC 160)|Pressure and argument|Silence|1|CCC 160, 2104–2109.
lessons.life: Pray for the grace to be sent.
lessons.saint: Francis Xavier: a Jesuit missionary who carried the Gospel to India and Japan.
misc: “Mission is only for those who go overseas.”
lessons.mem: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit… and behold, I am with you always.” (Matthew 28:19–20)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 28:19–20. Ask: “What are the verbs? What is the promise?” Go, make disciples, baptize, teach; and “I am with you always.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state their commitments to mission after graduation.

lessons.title: Review of the Creed
lessons.idea: The Creed is the summary of the faith. Reviewing it article by article helps students see how doctrine fits together and how it shapes life. Each student writes a commentary on the Creed in their own words.
lessons.question: What do I believe?
lessons.activity: “Write my own creed commentary” (50 min). Students choose two articles (e.g., “maker of heaven and earth”; “he descended to the dead”; “communion of saints”) and write a half-page each: what it says, Scripture, a Catechism reference, what difference it makes to my life. Recite the Creed together.
teach: The Creed organizes the faith: Father, Son, Holy Spirit and the Church (CCC 185–197). It is both a summary of faith and a personal profession.
The Creed has twelve articles in the Apostles’ Creed, traditionally attributed to the apostles (CCC 194). The Nicene Creed adds precision on Christ’s divinity and the Spirit.
Doctrine is connected to prayer and morals; lex orandi, lex credendi, lex vivendi.
Encourage students to pray the Creed regularly, e.g., at Mass, with attention.
quiz: The Apostles’ Creed is organized around…|Seven sacraments|Ten Commandments|The three Persons of the Trinity|Four marks|2|CCC 190.
The phrase “consubstantial with the Father” in the Nicene Creed teaches that…|The Son shares the same divine nature as the Father|Mary is divine|The Spirit is a force|The Son is a creature|0|CCC 242.

Why do we say “I believe” at Baptism but “We believe” at Mass?|It is accidental|The priests decide|Languages differ|Faith is personal and also shared with the whole Church (CCC 166–167)|3|CCC 166–167.
lessons.saint: Athanasius: bishop of Alexandria, who defended the divinity of Christ through repeated exiles.
misc: “The Creed is an old formula with no relevance.”
“I can pick which articles to believe.”
lessons.mem: “If you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” (Romans 10:9)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 10:9. Ask: “What do you confess with your lips? What do you believe in your heart?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to share one article of the Creed and what it means for their life.

lessons.title: Review of sacraments and morals
lessons.idea: This lesson integrates the sacraments and the moral life: grace received in the sacraments strengthens the life of love lived in the commandments and Beatitudes. Students present what they have learned and its coherence.
lessons.question: What changed?
lessons.activity: “Presentation” (50 min). In groups, students prepare a short presentation connecting a sacrament to a moral theme (Eucharist and justice; Penance and truth; Matrimony and chastity; Orders and service). They use Scripture, Catechism sections and a real-life example. Peers give feedback.
teach: The sacraments are the principal means of grace; the moral life is the response (CCC 1210–1211, 1716, 2052). Grace heals and elevates, the commandments and Beatitudes direct.
The Catechism has four pillars: Creed, sacraments, commandments, prayer. They interlock: what we believe, celebrate, live and pray.
Sacramental grace is not a license but a power: the Eucharist makes us one body and sends us.
Encourage students to find the thread through the whole course.
quiz: Grace and the moral life relate as…|Grace makes commandments unnecessary|Grace heals and strengthens us to live the commandments and Beatitudes|Only one matters|Law replaces grace|1|CCC 1996–2005.
The Catechism’s four parts correspond to…|Faith professed, celebrated, lived and prayed|Four councils|Genesis to Revelation|Four gospels|0|CCC 13–18.
Which sacrament strengthens us most directly for the moral life of charity?|None|The Eucharist, which makes us one body and sends us out|Only Baptism|Only Confirmation|1|CCC 1391–1397.
lessons.saint: Thomas Aquinas: the Dominican friar who wrote the Summa Theologiae and hymns for the Eucharist.
lessons.mem: “You shall love the Lord your God… and your neighbor as yourself.” (Matthew 22:37–39)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 22:37–40. Ask: “How do the sacraments help us live these two commands?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how a sacrament strengthens a moral virtue with a concrete example.

lessons.title: Capstone presentation
lessons.idea: The capstone is a final project in which students share what they have learned, how it has changed them and how they plan to live it, including a prayer. It is a chance to take ownership of faith as adults.
lessons.question: What is next?
lessons.activity: “Capstone project” (a week of preparation; 60 min sessions). Each student creates a project: a written reflection, a video, a service initiative, an artwork, or a teaching session. It includes: three key insights, one challenge or question, a plan for next steps and a prayer. Present to the class or parish, with a closing blessing.
teach: A capstone integrates learning, as in Catechism’s structure (CCC 2030). It invites personal appropriation: “faith seeking understanding.”
Include a plan: sacraments, service, study, community, mentor. A plan needs accountability.
The prayer is part of the work: thanksgiving, petition, offering.
Celebrate: an agape meal or a Mass of thanksgiving would be fitting.
quiz: A well-formed personal capstone plan includes…|Only ideas|Insights, a concrete plan, support and a prayer|A grade only|Nothing|1|Integrated learning leads to action.
Which best describes the aim of Christian formation?|Becoming disciples who know, celebrate, live and pray the faith|Memorizing facts only|Winning arguments|Earning credit|0|CCC 4–6.
After graduation, a student should stay connected to…|A single teacher|A parish, community and mentors|No one|Only social media|1|The faith is lived in the Church.
lessons.saint: Paul: “I press on.”
misc: “The end of the course is the end of formation.”
lessons.mem: “Forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal.” (Philippians 3:13–14)
lessons.hook: Read Philippians 3:12–14. Ask: “What does Paul mean by pressing on toward the goal?” Ask students what they hope to carry forward.
lessons.assess: Evaluate capstones using a rubric: accuracy, depth, personal engagement, concrete plan and prayer.

units.title: Hard questions: justice, science and salvation
units.eq: How do I hold to the faith when the issues are difficult?

lessons.title: The death penalty, war and peace
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that the death penalty is “inadmissible” today because of the dignity of the person, and that war may only be a last resort and must meet strict conditions.
lessons.question: Can killing ever be justified?
lessons.activity: Hold a structured debate using the just war criteria.
teach: In 2018 Pope Francis revised CCC 2267: the death penalty is “inadmissible” because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. Earlier editions allowed it in very rare cases if it was the only way to protect lives. The Church works for abolition.

Legitimate defense may require force (CCC 2263–2265) and bear grave responsibility. A war may only be just if: lasting, grave damage by an aggressor; all other means impractical; serious prospects of success; the use of arms does not produce greater evils (CCC 2309).
Conscientious objection is respected and those who serve are to see themselves as servants of peace (CCC 2310–2311).
Faithful Catholics argue about how to apply these principles. Study the criteria before taking a side.
talk: What does it mean that every life has dignity, even a murderer’s?
Is a “just war” possible in the age of nuclear weapons?
How should the justice owed to victims be balanced with mercy?
quiz: What did the 2018 revision of CCC 2267 say?|The Church takes no position|The death penalty is required|The death penalty is inadmissible|It is allowed whenever the state chooses|2|The revision.
Which is NOT one of the conditions for a just war?|A declaration by a popular vote|Lasting, grave damage by an aggressor|All other means impractical|Serious prospects of success|0|CCC 2309.
The Church’s view of conscientious objectors is that…|They deserve respect and a way to serve|They are heretics|They are always wrong|They must be punished|0|CCC 2311.
lessons.life: Read a short Church document on peace or the death penalty and share one question.
lessons.saint: Franz Jägerstätter: an Austrian farmer who refused to serve in the Nazi army and was executed in 1943.
misc: “The Church has always taught the death penalty is wrong.”
“Any war is justified if the government declares it.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the peacemakers.” (Matthew 5:9)
lessons.hook: Ask: “When is it right to use force? When is it never right?” List answers before the criteria.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state why the Church calls the death penalty inadmissible and apply the just war criteria to a case.

lessons.title: IVF, cloning and bioethics
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that children are a gift, not a product, and that science must serve the dignity of the person. It supports ethical treatments for infertility and rejects those that replace the marital act or destroy embryos.
lessons.question: Why does the Church say no to some fertility treatments?
lessons.activity: Compare ethical and unethical approaches in a table.
teach: The Church sympathizes deeply with couples who struggle with infertility (CCC 2374). It teaches that a child is a gift, not something owed or manufactured (CCC 2378).

In vitro fertilization separates procreation from the marital act and usually involves the creation and loss of embryos, so the Church holds that it is not morally acceptable (CCC 2377; Donum Vitae, 1987). Cloning and the destruction of embryos for research are rejected (CCC 2275).
Ethical options exist: restorative reproductive medicine, NFP-based fertility care, surgery and treatments that help the marital act, and also adoption and fostering and service (CCC 2379).
Adult stem cells and many other research paths are morally acceptable and effective.
talk: Why is it harder for a society to say “no” to technology that is wanted by many?
How can the Church speak with compassion to couples who have struggled with infertility?
What questions should we ask whenever science offers a new power?
quiz: A child conceived through IVF is…|A human person with full dignity|Less than human|Not loved by the Church|Not baptizable|0|The Church welcomes every child.
Which research is considered ethical?|None|Destroying embryos for stem cells|Cloning human embryos|Adult stem cell research|3|CCC 2275.
The Catechism’s advice to childless couples includes…|Pretending there is no pain|Adoption and service to others|Using any technology|Giving up on family|1|CCC 2379.
lessons.life: Pray for couples who are struggling to conceive or to adopt, and consider how you can support them.
lessons.saint: Gianna Beretta Molla: a doctor and mother, a patron of mothers and unborn children.
misc: “The Church is against all fertility treatments and all stem cell research.”
“A child conceived through IVF is not a person.”
lessons.mem: “Children are a heritage from the Lord, the fruit of the womb a reward.” (Psalm 127:3)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that infertility is a deep suffering for many couples. Begin with compassion.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why the Church distinguishes treatment from replacement of the marital act and name ethical options.

lessons.title: Is there salvation outside the Church?
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that salvation comes through Christ and his Church, yet that God can lead those who do not know the Gospel through no fault of their own to salvation. It does not say who is saved or lost.
lessons.question: Does the Church say non-Catholics go to hell?
lessons.activity: Read Lumen Gentium 16 and write what it says in your own words.
teach: “Outside the Church there is no salvation” means that all salvation comes from Christ through his Church (CCC 846). It does not mean everyone outside the visible Church is lost.

Those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ or his Church but seek God and try to do his will can be saved (CCC 847; Lumen Gentium 16). The Church does not say how, but trusts in God’s mercy (CCC 1260).
This is why mission is not optional: the Church has the fullness of the means of salvation, and love compels us to share the Gospel (CCC 848).
The Church recognizes truth and holiness in other religions (CCC 843; Nostra Aetate) and respects each person’s conscience.
talk: If God can save people outside the Church, why does the Church send missionaries?
How is the Catholic view different from “all religions are the same”?
How should we speak about our friends who belong to other religions or none?
quiz: According to CCC 847, who can be saved?|Only the Church’s leaders|Only baptized Catholics|Those who through no fault of their own do not know Christ but seek God|No one outside the Church|2|CCC 847.
The Church’s teaching on mission is that…|The Gospel must be shared out of love|It is only for priests|It is forbidden|It is optional|0|CCC 848.
What does the Church say about other religions?|They may contain truth and holiness|They are identical to Christianity|They are worthless|They should be abolished|0|CCC 843.
lessons.life: Have a respectful conversation with someone of a different faith, asking what matters most to them.
lessons.saint: Francis Xavier: a Jesuit missionary to India and Japan who lived among the people he served.
misc: “The Church teaches that all non-Catholics are going to hell.”
“All religions are equally true, so it doesn’t matter.”
lessons.mem: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” (John 14:6)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you think Catholics believe happens to people of other faiths?” Collect answers before reading the Catechism.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what the Church teaches about salvation outside the visible Church.

units.title: The moral life: acts, law and grace
units.eq: How do law and grace work together in a moral life?

lessons.title: The morality of human acts
lessons.idea: An act is good only if its object, intention and circumstances are good. The end does not justify the means. Passions and feelings are part of being human and are meant to be guided by reason.
lessons.question: What makes an act good or bad?
lessons.activity: Analyze cases using the three sources of morality (object, intention, circumstances). Write what changes if each one changes.
teach: The morality of an act depends on the object (what we choose), the intention (why), and the circumstances (CCC 1750–1754). All three must be good (CCC 1755).
A good intention does not make a bad act good; the end does not justify the means (CCC 1753, 1756; Romans 3:8). Some acts are always wrong (intrinsically evil) (CCC 1756).
Passions (love, fear, anger, joy) are not bad in themselves; they become good or evil depending on how reason guides them (CCC 1762–1770). Virtue orders the passions (CCC 1767–1770).
Circumstances can increase or lessen responsibility but cannot make a bad act good (CCC 1754).
talk: Which feelings are hardest to guide?
Can you think of a case where circumstances change responsibility?
quiz: The three sources of morality are…|Rules, fear, habit|Time, place, people|Feelings, plans, luck|Object, intention, circumstances|3|CCC 1750.
The end justifies the means is…|Sometimes right|Wrong|Right|Always right|1|CCC 1759.
Passions are…|Always good|Always bad|Irrelevant|Neither good nor bad in themselves|3|CCC 1767.
lessons.life: Choose one decision this week and examine its object, intention and circumstances.
lessons.saint: Thomas Aquinas: he wrote the clearest account of human acts and virtues.
lessons.mem: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” (Romans 12:21)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If someone steals to feed their family, is it good, bad or both?” Let students argue before introducing the three sources.
lessons.assess: Ask students to analyze a case with the three sources of morality.

lessons.title: Law: eternal, natural, Old and New
lessons.idea: God’s law is the plan of his wisdom. It is shown in the natural law written on our hearts, in the Old Law (Decalogue), and in the New Law of Christ, which is love and the grace of the Spirit.
lessons.question: How do natural law, Old Law and New Law relate?
lessons.activity: Create a chart with columns: eternal law, natural law, Old Law, New Law, civil law. Fill in definitions, sources, purposes and examples. Discuss how civil laws can be just or unjust.
teach: The eternal law is God’s plan for the universe (CCC 1950). The natural law is the participation of the rational creature in it, “the light of understanding placed in us by God” (CCC 1954–1960).
The Old Law is a preparation for the Gospel; the Decalogue states what reason can know (CCC 1961–1964). The New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit, the law of love and freedom (CCC 1965–1974).
Civil laws bind in conscience when they are just; an unjust law does not oblige (CCC 1902, 2242). Conscientious objection is a duty when laws require evil.
Jesus fulfills the law (Matthew 5:17). The Sermon on the Mount is its charter (CCC 1966).
talk: What is the difference between a rule and a law of love?
When might a civil law conflict with natural law?
How does grace change the way we keep the law?
quiz: Natural law is…|A civil law|Moral law known by reason|A feeling|A custom|1|CCC 1954.
The New Law is…|Mere suggestion|The grace of the Holy Spirit and love|Optional|A new set of rules|1|CCC 1966.
An unjust civil law…|Does not bind in conscience|Is divine|Is fine|Always binds|0|CCC 1903.
lessons.life: Read the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) over three days and note one way to live it.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: he defended conscience against an unjust law.
misc: “Natural law is only a Catholic idea.”
“The New Law abolishes the Ten Commandments.”
lessons.mem: “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free.” (Romans 8:2)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How do you know some things are wrong even without a rule?” Introduce natural law.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the relationship of the four laws.

lessons.title: Grace, justification and merit
lessons.idea: Grace is God’s free gift that makes us his children. Justification forgives sin and makes us holy. We cooperate with grace, and God rewards what he himself begins in us.
lessons.question: How do grace and effort work together?
lessons.activity: Study the Catholic and Lutheran agreement in the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999). Write a one-page statement on grace and works, with quotes from Scripture and the Catechism.
teach: Justification is God’s gift, removing sin and communicating righteousness through faith and Baptism (CCC 1987–1995). Its source is God’s mercy and Christ’s sacrifice (CCC 1992).

Grace is “the free and undeserved help that God gives us” (CCC 1996). Sanctifying grace makes us holy; actual grace helps us act (CCC 1999–2000). The Spirit works in us “both to will and to work” (Philippians 2:13).
Merit: we cannot earn the first grace, but God’s grace enables us to merit further graces and eternal life (CCC 2006–2011). Holiness is the fullness of Christian life (CCC 2012–2016).
The 1999 Joint Declaration on Justification shows Catholics and Lutherans share a basic consensus.
talk: Why is grace a gift and not a wage?
What does “work out your salvation with fear and trembling” mean?
How should we speak about grace with Protestant friends?
quiz: Grace is…|A reward for deeds|A wage|A feeling|A free and undeserved gift|3|CCC 1996.
Can we earn the first grace?|Never needed|Sometimes|Yes, by good works|No, it is a gift|3|CCC 2010.
The Joint Declaration on Justification was signed in…|2020|1999|1517|1965|1|CCC context.
lessons.life: Thank God for a gift you did not earn and respond with a concrete act of love.
lessons.saint: Thérèse of Lisieux: she called her “little way” a path of trust in grace.
lessons.mem: “For by grace you have been saved through faith.” (Ephesians 2:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Can you earn a gift? What do you do with one?” Use gifts to introduce grace.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain justification, grace and merit in their own words.

units.title: The tradition of prayer
units.eq: How does the Church teach us to pray?

lessons.title: The Psalms and Mary at prayer
